---
title: "Linear Algebra III: Spectral Theory and Quadratic Forms"
---

## Why spectral theory matters for indirect comparison {#sec-la3-intro}

The first two linear-algebra chapters built the stage: vector spaces, linear maps, rank, the four
fundamental subspaces (@thm-four-subspaces), orthogonality, and the projection theorem
(@thm-projection-theorem). Those chapters answer questions about *where* vectors live and *how* to
project onto a subspace. The present chapter answers a different and deeper question: given a linear
map represented by a matrix, are there special directions along which the map acts simply, by mere
scaling? The answer, for the symmetric matrices that dominate statistics, is an emphatic yes, and the
resulting *spectral theorem* is arguably the single most useful structural result in applied
mathematics.

Every quantity that controls the precision of an indirect treatment comparison is, at bottom, an
eigenvalue or a singular value of some matrix.

- The covariance matrix of an estimator, for instance $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$ for a
  vector of regression coefficients, is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Its eigenvalues are the
  variances of the estimator along its principal axes, and the variance of any linear contrast
  $\mathbf{a}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$, which is exactly the form an indirect-comparison estimand
  takes, is the quadratic form $\mathbf{a}^\top\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\,\mathbf{a}$.
- The Gram matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ of a design must be positive definite for the
  least-squares and maximum-likelihood problems of later chapters to have a unique well-conditioned
  solution. When it is only positive semidefinite, because covariates are collinear or because a study
  reports fewer data points than parameters, the *singular value decomposition* and the *Moore-Penrose
  pseudoinverse* of this chapter supply the minimum-norm solution that the inverse can no longer
  provide.
- The *matrix square root*, also constructed here, whitens correlated data: it turns a general
  covariance into the identity. This is the algebraic backbone of standardization, of the Mahalanobis
  distance used by the matching and distance methods of Part V, and of the Gaussian-copula
  constructions used for numerical integration.

We develop the theory in dependency order. We begin with eigenvalues, eigenvectors, the characteristic
polynomial, and diagonalization for a general square matrix. We then specialize to symmetric matrices,
proving the spectral theorem in full. From the spectral theorem we read off the theory of quadratic
forms and positive definiteness, the variational (Rayleigh) characterization of eigenvalues, the
singular value decomposition, the pseudoinverse, and the matrix square root. We close by noting that
covariance matrices are symmetric and positive semidefinite, which is the bridge into the probability
chapter (@thm-cov-psd). Throughout, the reference for standard linear-algebra background is
@strang2016.

### A running example we will reuse at every step

Before any abstraction, here is a small, concrete object to keep in mind. We will return to it after
almost every definition and theorem, so that each piece of machinery has an immediate meaning you can
check by hand.

::: {#exm-la3-contrast-covariance}
## Two correlated treatment-effect estimates

Two trials share a common comparator $A$. The first reports the log odds ratio of treatment $B$ versus
$A$, with estimate $\hat y_{AB}$; the second reports the log odds ratio of $C$ versus $A$, with estimate
$\hat y_{AC}$. When the two relative effects are estimated together in a network, the estimates are
correlated. Suppose their joint covariance matrix, in convenient units chosen to keep the arithmetic
clean, is
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{Cov}\!\begin{pmatrix}\hat y_{AB}\\ \hat y_{AC}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.
$$
The Bucher indirect comparison of $C$ versus $B$ is the contrast
$\hat d_{BC}=\hat y_{AB}-\hat y_{AC}$, which is $\mathbf{a}^\top(\hat y_{AB},\hat y_{AC})^\top$ for the
contrast vector $\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^\top$. Everything an indirect comparison cares about, namely the
uncertainty of $\hat d_{BC}$ and the directions of large and small uncertainty in
$(\hat y_{AB},\hat y_{AC})$, will turn out to be an eigenvalue, an eigenvector, or a quadratic form of
this one matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This is exactly the matrix carried through the fully worked example at the end of the chapter
(@sec-la3-example), so the threads tie together there.

### What each object in this chapter means for an indirect comparison

The chapter introduces a dozen linear-algebra objects. The following table is a map from each object to
the statistical role it plays, so that you always know why it is in the book. Skim it now and refer back
to it; nothing here needs to be understood yet.

| Object (this chapter) | What it is | Role in regression, NMA, or ITC |
|---|---|---|
| eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ | a scaling factor of the matrix | variance along a principal axis of an estimator |
| eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_i$ | a direction the matrix only scales | a principal direction of uncertainty or of covariate variation |
| quadratic form $\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}$ | a weighted sum of squares | the variance of a contrast such as the indirect estimate $\hat d_{BC}$ |
| positive definite $A\succ 0$ | every direction has positive value | every contrast has strictly positive variance; normal equations have a unique solution |
| spectral decomposition $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ | rotation to independent axes | principal component analysis of a covariance matrix |
| singular value $\sigma_i$ | a stretching factor of a rectangular matrix | how well the data support a model direction |
| SVD $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ | rotate, stretch, rotate | structure theorem for a design matrix |
| condition number $\sigma_1/\sigma_r$ | ratio of largest to smallest stretch | how much collinearity inflates the variance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ |
| pseudoinverse $A^{+}$ | best stand-in for an inverse | solves least squares when the design is collinear or rank-deficient |
| matrix square root $A^{1/2}$ | a symmetric square root | whitening and the Mahalanobis distance of Part V |

### Which results are core and which are deeper support

Not every result below carries the same weight for the rest of the book. On a first reading, focus on
the core results; the supporting ones can be taken on faith and revisited later.

| Result | Priority | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Spectral theorem (@thm-spectral-theorem) | core | every covariance and information matrix decomposes into independent axes |
| Definiteness and its eigenvalue test (@thm-pd-characterization) | core | positive definiteness is the condition for unique, stable estimation |
| Quadratic forms (@def-quadratic-form) | core | contrast variances are quadratic forms |
| Matrix square root (@prp-matrix-square-root) | core | whitening and Mahalanobis distance |
| Singular value decomposition (@thm-svd) | core | the structure theorem for rectangular design matrices |
| Pseudoinverse (@def-pseudoinverse) | core | least squares without an invertible Gram matrix |
| Covariance bridge (@sec-la3-covariance) | core | connects all of the above to statistics |
| Rayleigh quotient (@thm-rayleigh) | core | variance in a chosen direction; entry point to PCA |
| Trace and determinant from the spectrum (@lem-trace-det-eigenvalues) | supporting | total and generalized variance, used in summaries |
| Sylvester's criterion (@thm-sylvester-criterion) | supporting | a cheap arithmetic check for positive definiteness |
| Courant-Fischer min-max (@thm-courant-fischer) | supporting | interior eigenvalues, stability, and dimension reduction |

## Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and the characteristic polynomial {#sec-la3-eigen}

**Why care about eigenvalues at all.** When a matrix $A$ describes how some system transforms vectors,
most directions get both rotated and stretched, which is hard to picture. An *eigenvector* is a special
direction that the matrix only stretches, never rotates; the stretch factor is its *eigenvalue*. In
statistics the "system" is a covariance or information matrix, and its eigenvectors are the independent
axes of variation, with the eigenvalues telling us how much variance lies along each axis. For the
running covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ of @exm-la3-contrast-covariance, we will find one axis along
which the two estimates vary a lot together and one along which they vary little; those axes are the
eigenvectors and the amounts are the eigenvalues.

Because a real matrix can fail to have real eigenvalues, the cleanest setting in which to define
eigenvalues is the complex one. We work with $\mathbb{C}^n$, equipped with the conjugate-linear inner
product $\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle = \mathbf{x}^*\mathbf{y}$, where $\mathbf{x}^* =
\bar{\mathbf{x}}^\top$ is the conjugate transpose. Every real matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is in
particular a complex matrix, so the definitions below apply to it.

::: {.remark}
**A one-paragraph complex-number refresher (you can skip the details).** A complex number $z=a+bi$ has
conjugate $\bar z=a-bi$, and $z\bar z=a^2+b^2\ge 0$ is its squared magnitude. For a complex vector
$\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)^\top$, the **conjugate transpose** $\mathbf{x}^*=\bar{\mathbf{x}}^\top$ is
the row vector of conjugates. We use it instead of the plain transpose because
$\mathbf{x}^*\mathbf{x}=\sum_i \bar{x}_i x_i=\sum_i |x_i|^2\ge 0$ is a genuine squared length, whereas
$\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}=\sum_i x_i^2$ could be negative or even complex. That is the only reason the
conjugate appears. The good news for a health researcher: the matrices we actually care about, namely
symmetric covariance and Fisher information matrices, always have *real* eigenvalues and *real*
eigenvectors (we prove this in @lem-sym-real-eigenvalues), so the complex numbers are a temporary
technical device that disappears the moment we specialize to symmetric matrices. For a real matrix the
conjugate transpose $A^*$ is just the ordinary transpose $A^\top$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-eigenvalue}
## Eigenvalue and eigenvector

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. A scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ is an **eigenvalue** of $A$ if there
exists a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{C}^n$ with
$$
A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}.
$$
Any such $\mathbf{v}$ is an **eigenvector** of $A$ associated with $\lambda$. For a fixed eigenvalue
$\lambda$, the set
$$
E_\lambda = \{\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{C}^n : A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\} = \mathcal{N}(A-\lambda I)
$$
is the **eigenspace** of $\lambda$; it is a subspace. The set of all eigenvalues is the **spectrum** of
$A$, written $\mathrm{spec}(A)$.
:::

The dimension of the eigenspace is itself a named quantity that we will use repeatedly. To avoid burying
it, we state it on its own.

::: {#def-geometric-multiplicity}
## Geometric multiplicity

The **geometric multiplicity** of an eigenvalue $\lambda$ is the dimension $\dim E_\lambda\ge 1$ of its
eigenspace, that is, the number of linearly independent eigenvectors associated with $\lambda$.
:::

**Reader translation.** An eigenvector is a direction on which $A$ acts as plain multiplication by a
number, the eigenvalue. The eigenspace collects every such direction for one fixed eigenvalue, and the
geometric multiplicity counts how many genuinely independent such directions there are. For a covariance
matrix, an eigenvalue is a variance and its eigenvector is the direction in which that variance is felt.

To see the definition work, take the running matrix
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and the candidate direction
$\mathbf{v}=(1,1)^\top$. Then
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}=3\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=3\,\mathbf{v},
$$
so $(1,1)^\top$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $3$: along the direction where both estimates move
together, the variance is large. We will find the other eigenvalue, $1$, along $(1,-1)^\top$, which is
exactly the indirect-contrast direction.

The defining equation $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ rearranges to $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$.
A nonzero solution $\mathbf{v}$ exists if and only if $A-\lambda I$ is singular, that is, if and only
if $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. This turns the search for eigenvalues into a problem about a single
polynomial.

::: {#def-characteristic-polynomial}
## Characteristic polynomial

The **characteristic polynomial** of $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is
$$
\chi_A(t) = \det(tI - A).
$$ {#eq-char-poly}
:::

**Reader translation.** Finding eigenvalues by hand would mean searching all directions for one that
$A$ merely scales. The characteristic polynomial turns that geometric search into a single algebra
problem: its roots are exactly the eigenvalues. For a $2\times 2$ matrix this is just a quadratic, which
is why our running example is solvable on paper.

By the Leibniz expansion of the determinant, $\chi_A$ is a monic polynomial in $t$ of degree exactly
$n$, with real coefficients when $A$ is real. The next lemma is the bridge between the algebraic object
$\chi_A$ and the geometric object $E_\lambda$.

::: {#lem-eigen-char-poly}
## Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial

For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$, the scalar $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of
$A$ if and only if $\chi_A(\lambda)=0$. Consequently $A$ has at least one and at most $n$ distinct
eigenvalues, and counted with the multiplicities defined by the factorization
$\chi_A(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n (t-\lambda_i)$ it has exactly $n$ eigenvalues in $\mathbb{C}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @def-eigenvalue, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue if and only if $\mathcal{N}(A-\lambda I)\ne\{\mathbf{0}\}$,
that is, if and only if $A-\lambda I$ is not invertible. A square matrix is invertible if and only if
its determinant is nonzero (a standard fact about determinants; see @strang2016). Hence $\lambda$ is an
eigenvalue if and only if $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. Since $\det(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\det(\lambda I - A) =
(-1)^n\chi_A(\lambda)$, this is equivalent to $\chi_A(\lambda)=0$.

The polynomial $\chi_A$ has degree $n$, so it has at most $n$ distinct roots. By the fundamental
theorem of algebra it factors over $\mathbb{C}$ as $\chi_A(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n (t-\lambda_i)$ with the
$\lambda_i\in\mathbb{C}$ repeated according to multiplicity, giving exactly $n$ eigenvalues counted
this way. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This lemma is what makes eigenvalues computable: every variance axis of a
covariance matrix, every curvature of a log-likelihood, is a root of one polynomial. An $n\times n$
matrix has exactly $n$ eigenvalues (with repeats), so an estimator with $n$ parameters has exactly $n$
principal variance directions to account for.

The multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root of $\chi_A$ is the **algebraic multiplicity** of $\lambda$. The
geometric and algebraic multiplicities need not agree, but they are ordered.

::: {#lem-geo-le-alg}
## Geometric multiplicity does not exceed algebraic multiplicity

For every eigenvalue $\lambda_0$ of $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$,
$$
1 \le \dim E_{\lambda_0} \le (\text{algebraic multiplicity of } \lambda_0).
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $g=\dim E_{\lambda_0}\ge 1$ and choose a basis $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_g$ of $E_{\lambda_0}$.
Extend it to a basis $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_n$ of $\mathbb{C}^n$ (every linearly independent
set extends to a basis; see @def-basis and @strang2016) and assemble the columns into an invertible
matrix $S=[\mathbf{v}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{v}_n]$. Because $A\mathbf{v}_i=\lambda_0\mathbf{v}_i$ for
$i\le g$, the matrix $S^{-1}AS$ is block upper triangular,
$$
S^{-1}AS = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_0 I_g & B \\ \mathbf{0} & C \end{pmatrix},
$$
for some blocks $B$ and $C$. To see why the lower-left block is zero, read $S^{-1}AS$ column by column.
Its first $g$ columns are $S^{-1}(A\mathbf{v}_i)=S^{-1}(\lambda_0\mathbf{v}_i)=\lambda_0\,S^{-1}\mathbf{v}_i
=\lambda_0\mathbf{e}_i$ for $i\le g$, because $S^{-1}\mathbf{v}_i=\mathbf{e}_i$ (the $i$-th column of
$S^{-1}S=I$). The vector $\lambda_0\mathbf{e}_i$ has zeros in rows $g+1,\dots,n$, so the first $g$
columns of $S^{-1}AS$ are exactly the first $g$ columns of $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_0 I_g, C)$ with $B$
sitting on top; that is the displayed block form. Similar matrices share a characteristic polynomial,
since
$\det(tI - S^{-1}AS) = \det\!\big(S^{-1}(tI-A)S\big)=\det(tI-A)$ by multiplicativity of the
determinant. The determinant of a block upper-triangular matrix is the product of the determinants of
its diagonal blocks, so
$$
\chi_A(t) = \det(tI - S^{-1}AS) = (t-\lambda_0)^g\,\det(tI_{n-g}-C).
$$
Thus $(t-\lambda_0)^g$ divides $\chi_A$, so the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda_0$ is at least $g$.
$\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** The gap between the two multiplicities is exactly the trouble. When the geometric
multiplicity is strictly smaller than the algebraic one, a repeated eigenvalue does not supply enough
independent directions to build a coordinate system, and the matrix cannot be diagonalized. The spectral
theorem (@thm-spectral-theorem) will show that this pathology never occurs for symmetric matrices, which
is why covariance and information matrices are always so well behaved.

Eigenvectors belonging to *distinct* eigenvalues carry independent information. The following lemma is
the engine behind diagonalization.

::: {#lem-eigvec-independent}
## Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent

Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k$ be distinct eigenvalues of $A$ with associated eigenvectors
$\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$. Then $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ are linearly independent.
:::

::: {.proof}
We argue by induction on $k$. For $k=1$ the single eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1$ is nonzero, hence
independent. Assume the claim for $k-1$ and suppose
$$
c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}.
\tag{$\ast$}
$$
Apply $A$ to ($\ast$) and use $A\mathbf{v}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{v}_i$:
$$
c_1\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_k\lambda_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}.
$$
Subtract $\lambda_k$ times ($\ast$) from this equation; the $\mathbf{v}_k$ term cancels, leaving
$$
c_1(\lambda_1-\lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_{k-1}(\lambda_{k-1}-\lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_{k-1}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$
By the inductive hypothesis $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_{k-1}$ are independent, so each coefficient
vanishes: $c_i(\lambda_i-\lambda_k)=0$ for $i\le k-1$. Since the eigenvalues are distinct,
$\lambda_i-\lambda_k\ne 0$, forcing $c_i=0$ for $i\le k-1$. Then ($\ast$) reduces to
$c_k\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0}$, and $\mathbf{v}_k\ne\mathbf{0}$ gives $c_k=0$. All coefficients vanish, so
the eigenvectors are independent. $\square$
:::

## Diagonalization {#sec-la3-diag}

::: {#def-diagonalizable}
## Diagonalizable and similar matrices

Two matrices $A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ are **similar** if $B=S^{-1}AS$ for some invertible
$S\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ (or $\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$). The matrix $A$ is **diagonalizable** if it
is similar to a diagonal matrix, that is, if there exist an invertible $S$ and a diagonal $D$ with
$S^{-1}AS=D$.
:::

**Reader translation.** Two similar matrices are the *same* linear map written in two coordinate
systems; $S$ is the dictionary that translates between them. (Similarity is an equivalence relation, and
similar matrices share rank, determinant, trace, and spectrum, so these quantities describe the map, not
the coordinates.) To diagonalize is to find a coordinate system in which the map acts independently along
each axis: no axis leaks into another, and the map is just a list of scalings. That is the cleanest
possible description of a matrix, and the rest of the chapter is about when it is achievable.

::: {#thm-diagonalization-criterion}
## Diagonalization criterion

A matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is diagonalizable if and only if $\mathbb{C}^n$ has a basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $A$, equivalently if and only if $A$ has $n$ linearly independent
eigenvectors. When $S=[\mathbf{s}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{s}_n]$ has these eigenvectors as columns, then
$S^{-1}AS=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, where $A\mathbf{s}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{s}_i$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $A$ is diagonalizable, with $S^{-1}AS=D=\mathrm{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)$ for an invertible $S$
with columns $\mathbf{s}_1,\dots,\mathbf{s}_n$. Multiplying on the left by $S$ gives $AS=SD$. Reading
this equality column by column, $A\mathbf{s}_i=d_i\mathbf{s}_i$ for each $i$. Because $S$ is invertible
its columns are linearly independent and nonzero, so each $\mathbf{s}_i$ is an eigenvector and they form
a basis of $\mathbb{C}^n$.

Conversely, suppose $\mathbf{s}_1,\dots,\mathbf{s}_n$ are linearly independent eigenvectors,
$A\mathbf{s}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{s}_i$. Form $S=[\mathbf{s}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{s}_n]$, which is invertible
because its columns are independent. Then the $i$-th column of $AS$ is $A\mathbf{s}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{s}_i$,
which is the $i$-th column of $S\Lambda$ with $\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$. Hence
$AS=S\Lambda$, so $S^{-1}AS=\Lambda$ is diagonal. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** Diagonalizability is not symbol manipulation; it is the existence of a coordinate
system in which the matrix becomes a diagonal list of eigenvalues. Once we reach symmetric matrices, this
coordinate system will be an orthonormal one (a pure rotation), which is what lets us interpret a
covariance matrix as independent variances along perpendicular axes.

::: {#cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable}
## Distinct eigenvalues force diagonalizability

If $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ has $n$ distinct eigenvalues, then $A$ is diagonalizable.
:::

::: {.proof}
Choose one eigenvector for each of the $n$ distinct eigenvalues. By @lem-eigvec-independent these $n$
eigenvectors are linearly independent, so they form a basis of $\mathbb{C}^n$. Apply
@thm-diagonalization-criterion. $\square$
:::

The converse of the corollary is false, and not every matrix is diagonalizable.

::: {#def-defective}
## Defective matrix

A matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is **defective** if it does not have $n$ linearly independent
eigenvectors, equivalently if some eigenvalue has geometric multiplicity strictly less than its
algebraic multiplicity. By @thm-diagonalization-criterion a defective matrix is not diagonalizable.
:::

**Reader translation.** A defective matrix has a repeated eigenvalue that did not bring enough
independent directions with it, so there is no full set of axes to diagonalize in. The next example
shows the smallest one. The payoff of the spectral theorem is that symmetric matrices, and therefore all
covariance and information matrices, are *never* defective.

::: {.remark}
Distinct eigenvalues are sufficient but not necessary: the identity $I_n$ has the single eigenvalue $1$
with multiplicity $n$ yet is already diagonal. Diagonalizability can also fail outright. The matrix
$$
N=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
has $\chi_N(t)=t^2$, so its only eigenvalue is $0$ with algebraic multiplicity $2$, but
$E_0=\mathcal{N}(N)=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{e}_1\}$ has dimension $1$. The geometric multiplicity is
strictly less than the algebraic multiplicity, so $N$ has only one independent eigenvector and, by
@thm-diagonalization-criterion, is **not** diagonalizable; it is defective in the sense of
@def-defective. The spectral theorem below shows that symmetric matrices are never defective.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Trace and determinant as symmetric functions of the eigenvalues {#sec-la3-trace-det}

Two scalar summaries of a matrix, the trace $\mathrm{tr}(A)=\sum_i a_{ii}$ and the determinant
$\det(A)$, turn out to be the simplest symmetric functions of the eigenvalues. These two numbers are not
idle curiosities for a statistician. For a covariance matrix the trace is the *total variance* (the sum
of the variances along the principal axes), and the determinant is the *generalized variance*, which is
the squared volume of the confidence ellipsoid. The results below say both are read directly off the
eigenvalues, which is exactly why principal component analysis can speak of the share of total variance
"explained" by each axis. We first record a small but heavily used fact.

::: {#lem-trace-cyclic}
## Cyclic invariance of the trace

For $B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$,
$\mathrm{tr}(BC)=\mathrm{tr}(CB)$. In particular $\mathrm{tr}(S^{-1}AS)=\mathrm{tr}(A)$, so the trace is
a similarity invariant.
:::

::: {.proof}
Compute directly:
$$
\mathrm{tr}(BC)=\sum_{i=1}^m (BC)_{ii}=\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n B_{ij}C_{ji}
=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^m C_{ji}B_{ij}=\sum_{j=1}^n (CB)_{jj}=\mathrm{tr}(CB).
$$
Applying this with $B=S^{-1}A$ and $C=S$ gives $\mathrm{tr}(S^{-1}AS)=\mathrm{tr}(ASS^{-1})=\mathrm{tr}(A)$.
$\square$
:::

::: {#lem-trace-det-eigenvalues}
## Trace and determinant from the spectrum

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ have eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\in\mathbb{C}$ listed with
algebraic multiplicity. Then
$$
\mathrm{tr}(A)=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i,
\qquad
\det(A)=\prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_i .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-eigen-char-poly we may factor $\chi_A(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n (t-\lambda_i)$. Expanding,
$$
\prod_{i=1}^n (t-\lambda_i) = t^n - \Big(\sum_i\lambda_i\Big)t^{n-1} + \cdots + (-1)^n\prod_i\lambda_i .
\tag{1}
$$
We now compute the same coefficients from $\chi_A(t)=\det(tI-A)$ using the Leibniz expansion
$$
\det(tI-A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^n\big(t\,\delta_{i,\pi(i)}-a_{i,\pi(i)}\big),
$$
where $S_n$ is the set of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. A factor $t\,\delta_{i,\pi(i)}-a_{i,\pi(i)}$
contains the variable $t$ only when $\pi(i)=i$, so the degree in $t$ of the term indexed by $\pi$ equals
the number of fixed points of $\pi$ (a permutation $\pi$ contributes one factor of $t$ for each index it
leaves fixed).

It helps to see the pattern for $n=2$ before the general count. There the two permutations are the
identity, contributing $(t-a_{11})(t-a_{22})=t^2-(a_{11}+a_{22})t+a_{11}a_{22}$, and the swap, with no
fixed points, contributing $-a_{12}a_{21}$ (degree $0$ in $t$). So $\chi_A(t)=t^2-\mathrm{tr}(A)\,t+
\det(A)$: the identity alone produces the $t^{n-1}$ coefficient, exactly the claim we now prove in
general.

*Constant term.* Set $t=0$: $\chi_A(0)=\det(-A)=(-1)^n\det(A)$. Comparing with (1) evaluated at $t=0$,
namely $(-1)^n\prod_i\lambda_i$, gives $\det(A)=\prod_i\lambda_i$.

*Coefficient of $t^{n-1}$.* A permutation contributes to $t^{n}$ or $t^{n-1}$ only if it has at least
$n-1$ fixed points. No permutation has exactly $n-1$ fixed points, because fixing $n-1$ of the $n$
symbols forces the last one to be fixed as well (a permutation is a bijection, so once $n-1$ outputs are
pinned the remaining input has only one possible output left). Hence the only contributor is the identity
permutation, whose term is $\prod_{i=1}^n (t-a_{ii})$. The coefficient of $t^{n-1}$ in this product is
$-\sum_i a_{ii}=-\mathrm{tr}(A)$. Comparing with (1), $\mathrm{tr}(A)=\sum_i\lambda_i$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** Read for a covariance matrix, this lemma says total variance
$\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\sum_i\lambda_i$ is the sum of the principal-axis variances, and
generalized variance $\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\prod_i\lambda_i$ is their product. A single zero
eigenvalue makes the determinant zero, the signature of a perfectly collinear direction with no
variation; principal component analysis "explains" variance precisely by reporting each $\lambda_i$ as a
share of $\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$.

For the symmetric matrices treated next, both identities have a one-line proof from the spectral
decomposition $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$: by @lem-trace-cyclic, $\mathrm{tr}(A)=\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda Q^\top
Q)=\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda)=\sum_i\lambda_i$, and by multiplicativity of the determinant together with
$\det(Q)^2=\det(Q^\top Q)=\det(I)=1$, $\det(A)=\det(Q)\det(\Lambda)\det(Q^\top)=\det(\Lambda)=\prod_i\lambda_i$.

## Symmetric matrices and the spectral theorem {#sec-la3-spectral}

Recall from Chapter 2 that a matrix $Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is **orthogonal** if $Q^\top Q=I_n$,
equivalently $QQ^\top=I_n$, equivalently the columns of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Orthogonal matrices preserve inner products and norms: $\langle Q\mathbf{x},Q\mathbf{y}\rangle =
\mathbf{x}^\top Q^\top Q\mathbf{y}=\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle$. A matrix $A$ is **symmetric**
if $A^\top=A$.

Symmetric matrices are the best-behaved matrices in all of linear algebra. We prove three facts in
sequence: their eigenvalues are real, eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are automatically
orthogonal, and there is always a full orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. The last statement is the
spectral theorem.

**Why this matters, stated up front.** It is worth knowing the payoff before grinding through the proof.
The spectral theorem is the reason every covariance matrix can be rotated into independent variances
(this is principal component analysis), the reason a covariance matrix has a well-defined square root
(this is whitening and the Mahalanobis distance), and the reason the quadratic forms of the next section
reduce to simple weighted sums of squares. Because $A^\top=A$ describes covariance, correlation, Gram,
Hessian, and Fisher information matrices alike, this one theorem underwrites almost every precision
calculation in the book. (A reminder of two symbols from the [Notation](/notation.qmd) chapter:
$\mathcal{N}(A)$ is the null space of $A$ and $\mathcal{C}(A)$ is its column space.)

::: {#lem-sym-real-eigenvalues}
## Real eigenvalues and a real eigenvector

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric. Then every eigenvalue of $A$ is real, and every
eigenvalue has a real eigenvector.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ be an eigenvalue with eigenvector $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{C}^n$,
$\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}$. Consider the scalar $\mathbf{v}^*A\mathbf{v}$, where $\mathbf{v}^*=
\bar{\mathbf{v}}^\top$. Because $A$ is real and symmetric, $A^*=\bar A^\top=A^\top=A$ (for a real matrix
the conjugate transpose is just the transpose), so, using that the conjugate transpose of a product
reverses the order, $(\mathbf{v}^*A\mathbf{v})^* = \mathbf{v}^*A^*(\mathbf{v}^*)^*$ with
$(\mathbf{v}^*)^*=\mathbf{v}$, giving
$$
(\mathbf{v}^*A\mathbf{v})^* = \mathbf{v}^*A^*\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}^*A\mathbf{v}.
$$
A scalar equal to its own conjugate is real, so $\mathbf{v}^*A\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}$. Likewise
$\mathbf{v}^*\mathbf{v}=\sum_i|v_i|^2=\|\mathbf{v}\|^2$ is a positive real number. From
$A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ we get $\mathbf{v}^*A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\,\mathbf{v}^*\mathbf{v}$, so
$$
\lambda = \frac{\mathbf{v}^*A\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}^*\mathbf{v}}
$$
is a ratio of two real numbers, hence real.

Since $\lambda$ is real and $A$ is real, the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is a real matrix that is singular (by
@lem-eigen-char-poly its determinant is zero). A real singular matrix has a nonzero real vector in its
null space, namely a real solution of the real homogeneous system $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$.
That vector is a real eigenvector for $\lambda$. $\square$
:::

::: {#lem-sym-orthogonal-eigenvectors}
## Orthogonality of eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, and let $A\mathbf{u}=\lambda\mathbf{u}$,
$A\mathbf{w}=\mu\mathbf{w}$ with $\lambda\ne\mu$. Then $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{w}=0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Using $A^\top=A$,
$$
\lambda\,\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{w}=(\lambda\mathbf{u})^\top\mathbf{w}=(A\mathbf{u})^\top\mathbf{w}
=\mathbf{u}^\top A^\top\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}^\top A\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}^\top(\mu\mathbf{w})
=\mu\,\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{w}.
$$
Hence $(\lambda-\mu)\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{w}=0$, and since $\lambda\ne\mu$ we conclude
$\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{w}=0$. $\square$
:::

We now prove the central theorem of the chapter. The proof is by induction on $n$ and uses only the
existence of one real eigenvector (@lem-sym-real-eigenvalues), the invariance of the orthogonal
complement, and the ability to extend an orthonormal set to an orthonormal basis (Gram-Schmidt,
@thm-gram-schmidt).

::: {#thm-spectral-theorem}
## Spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric. Then there exist an orthogonal matrix
$Q=[\mathbf{q}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{q}_n]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and a real diagonal matrix
$\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ such that
$$
A = Q\Lambda Q^\top = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\,\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^\top .
$$ {#eq-spectral-decomposition}
The columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_n$ form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of
eigenvectors of $A$, with $A\mathbf{q}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i$, and the $\lambda_i$ are exactly the
eigenvalues of $A$ repeated with multiplicity. In particular every real symmetric matrix is
diagonalizable, by an orthogonal change of basis, and is never defective.
:::

The proof is the longest in the chapter, so here is the plan before the details. It is an induction on
the size $n$, peeling off one eigenvector at a time.

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| Base case | a $1\times 1$ matrix is already diagonal |
| Step 1: first eigenvector | a real unit eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_1$ exists by @lem-sym-real-eigenvalues |
| Step 2: invariant complement | the hyperplane $\mathbf{q}_1^\perp$ is mapped into itself by $A$ |
| Step 3: shrink the problem | $A$ restricted to that hyperplane is a smaller symmetric matrix; apply the inductive hypothesis |
| Step 4: assemble | glue $\mathbf{q}_1$ to the smaller orthonormal eigenbasis to get the full one |

::: {.proof}
*Base case.* We induct on $n$. For $n=1$ the matrix $A=(a_{11})$ is already diagonal, with $Q=(1)$ and
$\Lambda=(a_{11})$.

*Step 1: the first eigenvector.* Assume the theorem for all symmetric matrices of size $n-1$, and let
$A$ be symmetric of size $n$. By @lem-sym-real-eigenvalues, $A$ has a real eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ with a
real eigenvector, which we scale to unit length: $A\mathbf{q}_1=\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1$,
$\|\mathbf{q}_1\|=1$.

*Step 2: the invariant complement.* Let
$$
W=\mathbf{q}_1^\perp=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:\mathbf{q}_1^\top\mathbf{x}=0\},
$$
a subspace of dimension $n-1$ by @thm-rank-nullity. The subspace $W$ is **$A$-invariant**, meaning that
once a vector lies in $W$, applying $A$ keeps it in $W$: if $\mathbf{x}\in W$ then, using symmetry,
$$
\mathbf{q}_1^\top(A\mathbf{x})=(A\mathbf{q}_1)^\top\mathbf{x}
=\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1^\top\mathbf{x}=0,
$$
so $A\mathbf{x}\in W$. This is what lets us reduce the problem to one dimension lower.

*Step 3: shrink the problem.* Recall $W$ has dimension $n-1$. By @thm-gram-schmidt choose an orthonormal
basis of $W$ and assemble it as the columns of a matrix
$Q_1\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-1)}$, so that $Q_1^\top Q_1=I_{n-1}$, the columns of $Q_1$ span $W$, and
$Q_1^\top\mathbf{q}_1=\mathbf{0}$ because the columns of $Q_1$ lie in $W=\mathbf{q}_1^\perp$. Define the
$(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix
$$
B=Q_1^\top A Q_1 .
$$
It is symmetric, since $B^\top=Q_1^\top A^\top Q_1=Q_1^\top A Q_1=B$. By the inductive hypothesis there
are an orthogonal $R\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}$ and a real diagonal
$\Lambda'=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n)$ with $B=R\Lambda'R^\top$.

*Step 4: assemble.* Set $\tilde Q=[\mathbf{q}_1\ \mid\ Q_1R]$. Its columns are orthonormal: $\mathbf{q}_1$ has unit norm, the
columns of $Q_1R$ have the form $Q_1\mathbf{r}$ for orthonormal $\mathbf{r}$ and satisfy
$(Q_1R)^\top(Q_1R)=R^\top Q_1^\top Q_1 R=R^\top R=I_{n-1}$, and they are orthogonal to $\mathbf{q}_1$
because $(Q_1R)^\top\mathbf{q}_1=R^\top Q_1^\top\mathbf{q}_1=\mathbf{0}$. Hence $\tilde Q$ is orthogonal.
Compute
$$
\tilde Q^\top A\tilde Q
=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{q}_1^\top A\mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_1^\top A Q_1 R\\
(Q_1R)^\top A\mathbf{q}_1 & (Q_1R)^\top A Q_1 R\end{pmatrix}.
$$
The diagonal scalar is $\mathbf{q}_1^\top A\mathbf{q}_1=\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1^\top\mathbf{q}_1=\lambda_1$.
The off-diagonal blocks vanish: since $A\mathbf{q}_1=\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1$ and $Q_1^\top\mathbf{q}_1=
\mathbf{0}$,
$$
(Q_1R)^\top A\mathbf{q}_1=R^\top Q_1^\top(\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1)=\lambda_1 R^\top Q_1^\top\mathbf{q}_1
=\mathbf{0},
$$
and the upper block is its transpose, also zero. The lower-right block is
$(Q_1R)^\top A(Q_1R)=R^\top(Q_1^\top A Q_1)R=R^\top B R=\Lambda'$. Therefore
$$
\tilde Q^\top A\tilde Q=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1 & \mathbf{0}^\top\\\mathbf{0}&\Lambda'\end{pmatrix}
=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n)=:\Lambda,
$$
which rearranges to $A=\tilde Q\Lambda\tilde Q^\top$. Taking $Q=\tilde Q$ completes the induction. The
identity $A=\sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^\top$ is the column-wise expansion of $Q\Lambda
Q^\top$, and reading $AQ=Q\Lambda$ column by column shows $A\mathbf{q}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i$, so each
$\mathbf{q}_i$ is an eigenvector and each $\lambda_i$ an eigenvalue. That the listed $\lambda_i$ are all
the eigenvalues with multiplicity follows because $\chi_A=\chi_\Lambda=\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)$ by
similarity. $\square$
:::

The expansion @eq-spectral-decomposition deserves a second reading, and the interpretation is important
enough to record as a proposition.

::: {#prp-spectral-projections}
## Spectral decomposition as a sum of orthogonal projections

Let $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ be a spectral decomposition of a symmetric matrix, with orthonormal eigenvectors
$\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_n$. Each rank-one matrix $P_i=\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^\top$ is the
orthogonal projection onto the eigenline $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{q}_i\}$, and
$$
A=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i P_i=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(A)}\lambda\,P_{E_\lambda},
$$
where $P_{E_\lambda}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace $E_\lambda$. The eigenspaces are
mutually orthogonal, and every vector of $\mathbb{R}^n$ splits uniquely into one piece in each
eigenspace.
:::

::: {.proof}
Each $P_i$ is symmetric and idempotent, $P_i^2=\mathbf{q}_i(\mathbf{q}_i^\top\mathbf{q}_i)
\mathbf{q}_i^\top=P_i$, so by the projection theorem (@thm-projection-theorem) and the
orthonormal-basis formula for an orthogonal projection matrix (@def-projection-matrix) it is exactly the
orthogonal projection onto $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{q}_i\}$. Summing the rank-one expansion
@eq-spectral-decomposition gives $A=\sum_i\lambda_i P_i$. Grouping the terms with a common eigenvalue
$\lambda$, the corresponding $\mathbf{q}_i$ span $E_\lambda$ and their rank-one projections add to
$P_{E_\lambda}$, yielding the grouped form. Distinct eigenspaces are orthogonal by
@lem-sym-orthogonal-eigenvectors, and since the $n$ eigenvectors form a basis, every vector decomposes
uniquely across the eigenspaces. (In the language of @sec-la3-spectral, this last property is summarized
by saying the eigenspaces form a **direct sum** equal to $\mathbb{R}^n$, written with the direct-sum
symbol as $\mathbb{R}^n=\bigoplus_\lambda E_\lambda$: a direct sum is a sum of subspaces in which each
vector has exactly one decomposition.) $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is the bridge from abstract algebra to geometry. A symmetric matrix is nothing
more than a set of perpendicular directions, each with a number attached: it scales the part of any
vector lying along $\mathbf{q}_i$ by $\lambda_i$ and adds the results. For a covariance matrix the
$\mathbf{q}_i$ are the principal axes of the data cloud and the $\lambda_i$ are the variances along them.

::: {.remark}
**Reader checkpoint.** If you retain one thing from this section, retain this: a symmetric matrix can be
rotated into a set of independent perpendicular axes; the eigenvalues tell you the strength, or variance,
along each axis; and nothing is lost in the rotation. This is precisely why covariance matrices, however
large, are manageable, and it is the engine of principal component analysis. The proofs above are there
for rigor; on a first reading you may use the result and move on. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

For the running covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ the proposition
reads, with $\mathbf{q}_+=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)^\top$ and $\mathbf{q}_-=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)^\top$,
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=3\,\mathbf{q}_+\mathbf{q}_+^\top+1\,\mathbf{q}_-\mathbf{q}_-^\top
=3\cdot\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}+1\cdot\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.
$$
The "both estimates move together" axis carries variance $3$; the indirect-contrast axis $(1,-1)$ carries
variance $1$ per unit length.

::: {.remark}
**Functions of a symmetric matrix.** Once $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ is in hand, any function
$f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined on the eigenvalues extends to $A$ by acting on the spectrum:
$$
f(A):=Q\,f(\Lambda)\,Q^\top,\qquad f(\Lambda)=\mathrm{diag}\big(f(\lambda_1),\dots,f(\lambda_n)\big).
$$
The idea is that $A$ does nothing but scale along its axes, so to apply a function to $A$ we apply the
function to those scalings and leave the axes alone. The smallest instance: if
$A=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(4,9)\,Q^\top$, then its square root is $A^{1/2}=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(2,3)\,Q^\top$ and its
inverse is $A^{-1}=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\tfrac14,\tfrac19)\,Q^\top$; one simply takes $\sqrt{\cdot}$ or
$1/(\cdot)$ of each eigenvalue. This is legitimate, and not just a convenient definition: it agrees with
the algebraic meaning whenever $f$ is a polynomial, because $A^k=Q\Lambda^k Q^\top$ (the $Q^\top Q=I$
in the middle collapses), and it is independent of the choice of $Q$ because $f(A)$ acts as
multiplication by $f(\lambda)$ on each eigenspace $E_\lambda$. We use the cases $f(t)=t^{-1}$ (the
inverse, when all $\lambda_i\ne 0$) and $f(t)=\sqrt{t}$ (the square root, when all $\lambda_i\ge 0$)
below. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Quadratic forms and definiteness {#sec-la3-quadratic}

::: {#def-quadratic-form}
## Quadratic form

A **quadratic form** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a function $q:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ of the shape
$$
q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_i x_j,
$$
where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. The matrix $A$ may always be taken symmetric, and the symmetric
matrix representing a given $q$ is unique.
:::

::: {.proof}
We justify the two claims in the definition. For any $M$, since $\mathbf{x}^\top M\mathbf{x}$ is a
scalar it equals its own transpose, $\mathbf{x}^\top M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^\top M^\top\mathbf{x}$, so
$$
\mathbf{x}^\top M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^\top\Big(\tfrac{M+M^\top}{2}\Big)\mathbf{x},
$$
and the **symmetric part** $\tfrac{1}{2}(M+M^\top)$ represents the same form. For uniqueness, suppose
symmetric matrices $A$ and $A'$ satisfy $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^\top A'\mathbf{x}$ for
all $\mathbf{x}$, and set $D=A-A'$, which is symmetric with $\mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf{x}=0$ for all
$\mathbf{x}$. Taking $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{e}_i$ gives $D_{ii}=0$; taking
$\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{e}_i+\mathbf{e}_j$ gives $D_{ii}+2D_{ij}+D_{jj}=0$, hence $D_{ij}=0$. So $D=0$ and
$A=A'$. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation.** A quadratic form is a weighted sum of squares and cross-products of the
coordinates; the matrix $A$ just stores the weights. The statistical instance to keep in mind is
$A=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$: the quadratic form $\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}$ is the
variance of the linear combination $\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{X}$ (we prove this in @sec-la3-covariance).
For our running example with $\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^\top$,
$$
\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=2-1-1+2=2,
$$
which is the variance of the indirect comparison $\hat d_{BC}=\hat y_{AB}-\hat y_{AC}$. Quadratic forms
are how every variance in this book is computed.

From now on the matrix of a quadratic form is symmetric. Definiteness classifies a symmetric matrix by
the sign of its quadratic form.

::: {#def-definiteness}
## Definiteness

A symmetric matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is

- **positive definite**, written $A\succ 0$, if $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}>0$ for every
  $\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}$;
- **positive semidefinite**, written $A\succeq 0$, if $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}\ge 0$ for every
  $\mathbf{x}$;
- **negative definite** ($A\prec 0$) or **negative semidefinite** ($A\preceq 0$) if $-A$ is positive
  definite or positive semidefinite;
- **indefinite** if $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}$ takes both signs.

For symmetric $A,B$ we write $A\succeq B$ to mean $A-B\succeq 0$, and likewise $A\succ B$.
:::

**Reader translation.** Definiteness is the sign of the quadratic form, read as a verdict on every
direction at once. Positive definite means every direction has strictly positive value: for a covariance
matrix, every contrast has strictly positive variance, and for a curvature (Hessian) matrix, the surface
curves up in every direction. Positive *semi*definite weakens this to "nonnegative", allowing a flat
direction; a flat direction in a covariance matrix is a linear combination with zero variance, that is, a
perfectly collinear direction. Indefinite means the form goes up in some directions and down in others, a
saddle. The smallest indefinite matrix is
$$
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{x}^\top B\mathbf{x}=x_1^2-x_2^2,
$$
with eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$; the form is positive along $\mathbf{e}_1$ and negative along
$\mathbf{e}_2$. The notation $A\succeq B$ extends the symbol $\succeq 0$ from the [Notation](/notation.qmd)
chapter: read $A\succeq B$ as "$A-B$ is positive semidefinite", which for covariance matrices means $A$ is
at least as variable as $B$ in every direction.

The spectral theorem reduces every question about a quadratic form to a question about signs of
eigenvalues, because an orthogonal change of variables turns the form into a weighted sum of squares.

::: {#thm-pd-characterization}
## Eigenvalue characterization of definiteness

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ (all real by
@lem-sym-real-eigenvalues). Then

1. $A\succ 0$ if and only if $\lambda_i>0$ for every $i$;
2. $A\succeq 0$ if and only if $\lambda_i\ge 0$ for every $i$;
3. $A$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both a positive and a negative eigenvalue.

Consequently a positive definite matrix is invertible with $\det(A)=\prod_i\lambda_i>0$, and a positive
semidefinite matrix has $\det(A)\ge 0$ and $\mathrm{tr}(A)\ge 0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ by @thm-spectral-theorem and change variables $\mathbf{y}=Q^\top\mathbf{x}$.
Because $Q$ is orthogonal, the map $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{y}$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with
$\mathbf{x}=Q\mathbf{y}$, and $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ if and only if $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$. Then
$$
\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^\top Q\Lambda Q^\top\mathbf{x}
=\mathbf{y}^\top\Lambda\mathbf{y}=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i y_i^2 .
$$ {#eq-quadratic-diagonalized}

*Claim 1.* If every $\lambda_i>0$ and $\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}$, then $\mathbf{y}\ne\mathbf{0}$, so
$\sum_i\lambda_i y_i^2>0$. Conversely, if some $\lambda_k\le 0$, take $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{q}_k$, the
$k$-th column of $Q$, so that $\mathbf{y}=Q^\top\mathbf{q}_k=\mathbf{e}_k$ and
$\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\lambda_k\le 0$ with $\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}$, contradicting positive
definiteness.

*Claim 2.* If every $\lambda_i\ge 0$ then $\sum_i\lambda_i y_i^2\ge 0$ for all $\mathbf{y}$. Conversely,
if some $\lambda_k<0$ then $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{q}_k$ gives $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\lambda_k<0$,
contradicting positive semidefiniteness.

*Claim 3.* By @eq-quadratic-diagonalized the range of $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}$ over
$\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}$ is contained in $[\min_i\lambda_i,\ \max_i\lambda_i]$ and contains both
endpoints (attained at the corresponding $\mathbf{q}_i$). It takes both signs if and only if
$\min_i\lambda_i<0<\max_i\lambda_i$, that is, if and only if $A$ has eigenvalues of both signs.

The final statements follow from @lem-trace-det-eigenvalues: $\det(A)=\prod_i\lambda_i$ and
$\mathrm{tr}(A)=\sum_i\lambda_i$, with the stated signs read off the eigenvalues. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This theorem turns "is every contrast informative?" into "are all eigenvalues
positive?". A positive definite covariance matrix means every contrast, including the indirect
comparison $\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^\top$, has strictly positive variance, and a positive definite Gram matrix
is exactly what makes the regression of Chapter 6 have a unique, stable solution. The borderline case is
the informative one: a zero eigenvalue (positive semidefinite but not definite) is the algebraic
fingerprint of a real data problem, namely a covariate direction carrying no independent information, a
collinear design matrix, or a linear combination of estimates with no variation at all.

::: {.remark}
The same change of variables proves a fact we use repeatedly: a symmetric matrix $A$ is positive
semidefinite if and only if $A=B^\top B$ for some matrix $B$, namely $B=\Lambda^{1/2}Q^\top$ when
$A\succeq 0$, while conversely $\mathbf{x}^\top B^\top B\mathbf{x}=\|B\mathbf{x}\|^2\ge 0$ always. The
Gram matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ of any matrix $\mathbf{X}$ is therefore positive semidefinite,
and it is positive definite exactly when $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank, since then
$\mathbf{X}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ forces $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$. This is the algebraic reason the normal
equations of Chapter 6 have a unique solution. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The eigenvalue test requires diagonalizing $A$, which means finding all its eigenvalues. A second, purely
arithmetic, test reads positive definiteness off determinants of small submatrices instead. This is worth
having because computing eigenvalues is hard (it is, in general, root-finding), whereas computing
determinants of small top-left blocks is easy and exact. First we name those submatrices.

::: {#def-principal-minor}
## Principal minors and leading principal minors

For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and an index set $\emptyset\ne S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$, the
**principal minor** indexed by $S$ is the determinant of the submatrix of $A$ keeping only the rows and
columns in $S$. The **leading principal minor** of order $k$ is the special case $S=\{1,\dots,k\}$,
namely $\Delta_k=\det(A_k)$ where $A_k$ is the top-left $k\times k$ submatrix.
:::

**Reader translation.** A leading principal minor just chops $A$ down to its top-left corner of a given
size and takes the determinant. "Leading" means the corner always starts at position $(1,1)$; a general
"principal" minor may use any subset of the coordinates, not just the first $k$. The distinction matters
below: the positive *definite* test needs only the leading minors, but the positive *semidefinite* test
needs all principal minors.

We prove the criterion in full. Plan of proof: the forward direction is a one-line restriction argument;
for the converse we induct on $n$, get $A_{n-1}\succ 0$ from the inductive hypothesis, and rule out a
negative eigenvalue by a dimension-count contradiction.

::: {#thm-sylvester-criterion}
## Sylvester's criterion (leading principal minors)

For a symmetric $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, let $A_k$ denote the top-left $k\times k$ submatrix and
$\Delta_k=\det(A_k)$ its leading principal minor, $k=1,\dots,n$. Then
$$
A\succ 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Delta_k>0 \text{ for every } k=1,\dots,n .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $A\succ 0$. Fix $k$ and let $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^k$ be nonzero. Pad it with
zeros to $\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{z}^\top,\mathbf{0}^\top)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$; then $\mathbf{x}\ne
\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{z}^\top A_k\mathbf{z}>0$. Hence $A_k\succ 0$, so by
@thm-pd-characterization all eigenvalues of $A_k$ are positive and $\Delta_k=\det(A_k)=\prod(\text{its
eigenvalues})>0$.

($\Leftarrow$) We induct on $n$. For $n=1$, $\Delta_1=a_{11}>0$ means $A=(a_{11})\succ 0$. Assume the
implication for symmetric matrices of size $n-1$, and suppose all leading principal minors of the
$n\times n$ matrix $A$ are positive. The leading principal minors of $A_{n-1}$ are exactly
$\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_{n-1}$, all positive, so by the inductive hypothesis $A_{n-1}\succ 0$. It remains
to upgrade this to $A\succ 0$ using $\det(A)=\Delta_n>0$.

Suppose, for contradiction, that $A$ is not positive definite. By @thm-spectral-theorem, $A$ has an
orthonormal eigenbasis $\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_n$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le
\lambda_n$. Since $\det(A)=\prod_i\lambda_i=\Delta_n>0$, no eigenvalue is zero. Since $A\not\succ 0$,
@thm-pd-characterization gives some $\lambda_i\le 0$, hence $\lambda_1<0$. A product of nonzero reals is
positive only with an even number of negative factors, so there are at least two negative eigenvalues;
thus $\lambda_2<0$ as well. Let
$$
U=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2\},\qquad V=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_n=0\}.
$$
The choice of $V$ is not special to the last coordinate: we only need *some* $(n-1)$-dimensional subspace
on which $A$ is positive definite, and the slice $x_n=0$ is one because restricting $A$ to it gives
$A_{n-1}\succ 0$. Any other such subspace would serve. On $U$ the form is negative and on $V$ it is
positive, and a dimension count will force these two subspaces to share a nonzero vector, the
contradiction. For nonzero $\mathbf{x}=c_1\mathbf{q}_1+c_2\mathbf{q}_2\in U$, orthonormality gives
$\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\lambda_1 c_1^2+\lambda_2 c_2^2<0$. For nonzero $\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{z}^\top,0)^\top\in V$,
we have $\mathbf{z}\ne\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{z}^\top A_{n-1}\mathbf{z}>0$
because $A_{n-1}\succ 0$. Now $\dim U=2$ and $\dim V=n-1$, so by the dimension formula for subspaces
(@thm-rank-nullity),
$$
\dim(U\cap V)\ge \dim U+\dim V-n = 2+(n-1)-n = 1 .
$$
Pick a nonzero $\mathbf{x}\in U\cap V$. Then $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}<0$ because $\mathbf{x}\in U$,
and $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}>0$ because $\mathbf{x}\in V$, a contradiction. Therefore $A\succ 0$,
completing the induction. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is the test you actually run on a small matrix by hand or quickly in code: to
check that an estimated covariance matrix, a Hessian, or a Fisher information matrix is positive definite,
compute a few determinants of top-left blocks rather than all the eigenvalues. It is a supporting result,
not a conceptual one; its value is computational convenience.

::: {.remark}
Sylvester's criterion is for *positive definiteness* only. The analogous statement for *positive
semidefiniteness* requires **all** principal minors to be nonnegative, not merely the leading ones; the
leading minors alone do not suffice, as the matrix $\mathrm{diag}(0,-1)$ shows, whose leading minors are
$0$ and $0$ yet which is not positive semidefinite. We use the eigenvalue characterization
(@thm-pd-characterization) whenever semidefiniteness is at issue. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We can now construct the matrix square root, the function $f(t)=\sqrt t$ from the remark above, and
prove that it is unique among symmetric positive semidefinite roots. Why would a statistician want the
square root of a matrix? Because $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ is the tool that *whitens* correlated data:
applying $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}$ to a random vector with covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ turns its
covariance into the identity, removing all correlation and unequal scaling. That same root defines the
Mahalanobis distance used by the matching methods of Part V. We construct it here and cash out both uses
in @sec-la3-covariance.

::: {#prp-matrix-square-root}
## Symmetric positive semidefinite square root

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. Then there is a unique symmetric
positive semidefinite matrix $A^{1/2}$ with $(A^{1/2})^2=A$, namely
$A^{1/2}=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\dots,\sqrt{\lambda_n})\,Q^\top$ for any spectral
decomposition $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$. If $A\succ 0$ then $A^{1/2}\succ 0$ and is invertible, and we write
$A^{-1/2}=(A^{1/2})^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Existence.* By @thm-pd-characterization, $A\succeq 0$ gives $\lambda_i\ge 0$, so $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ is
real. Put $S=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_i})\,Q^\top$. It is symmetric, its eigenvalues
$\sqrt{\lambda_i}\ge 0$ make it positive semidefinite, and
$$
S^2=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_i})\,Q^\top Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_i})\,Q^\top
=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_i)\,Q^\top=A .
$$

*Uniqueness.* Let $B$ be symmetric positive semidefinite with $B^2=A$. By @thm-spectral-theorem write
$B=\sum_j\mu_j\,\mathbf{p}_j\mathbf{p}_j^\top$ with $\mu_j\ge 0$ and $\{\mathbf{p}_j\}$ an orthonormal
basis. Orthonormality gives $B^2=\sum_j\mu_j^2\,\mathbf{p}_j\mathbf{p}_j^\top$, so $A=B^2$ has each
$\mathbf{p}_j$ as an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\mu_j^2$. The matrix $S=A^{1/2}$ constructed above acts
on each eigenvector of $A$ by multiplying by the nonnegative square root of the corresponding
eigenvalue, since $S$ restricts to $\sqrt{\lambda}\,\mathrm{Id}$ on each eigenspace $E_\lambda(A)$. Hence
$$
S\mathbf{p}_j=\sqrt{\mu_j^2}\,\mathbf{p}_j=\mu_j\mathbf{p}_j=B\mathbf{p}_j
$$
for every $j$. Two matrices that agree on the basis $\{\mathbf{p}_j\}$ are equal, so $B=S=A^{1/2}$.

If $A\succ 0$ then all $\lambda_i>0$, so all $\sqrt{\lambda_i}>0$, making $A^{1/2}$ positive definite
and invertible by @thm-pd-characterization. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** A unique symmetric positive semidefinite square root is what makes whitening
well defined: there is exactly one natural $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$, so the standardized vector
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ and the Mahalanobis distance built from it are
unambiguous. Standardization, the Mahalanobis distance, and the Gaussian-copula constructions of Part V
all rest on this one proposition.

## The Rayleigh quotient and the variational characterization of eigenvalues {#sec-la3-rayleigh}

The eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are not only roots of a polynomial; they are solutions of
optimization problems. The object that does the work is the Rayleigh quotient, which for a covariance
matrix answers a concrete question: "how much variance do I see if I look in this particular direction?".
The largest and smallest answers are the extreme eigenvalues, attained along the corresponding
eigenvectors. This variational viewpoint is what makes eigenvalues stable under perturbation and is the
entry point to principal component analysis and to the conditioning bounds used throughout statistics.

::: {#def-rayleigh-quotient}
## Rayleigh quotient

For a symmetric $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and $\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}$, the **Rayleigh quotient** is
$$
R_A(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}}.
$$
It is invariant under nonzero rescaling, $R_A(c\mathbf{x})=R_A(\mathbf{x})$ for $c\ne 0$, so it is
determined by the direction of $\mathbf{x}$ and equals $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}$ on the unit sphere
$\|\mathbf{x}\|=1$.
:::

**Reader translation.** Dividing by $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}=\|\mathbf{x}\|^2$ cancels the length of
$\mathbf{x}$, so the Rayleigh quotient depends only on the *direction* you point in. With $A=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ it is the variance per unit length in that direction. Sweeping the direction around,
the largest value you can reach is the top eigenvalue and the smallest is the bottom eigenvalue: the most
and least uncertain directions of the estimator.

::: {#thm-rayleigh}
## Variational characterization of the extreme eigenvalues

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues ordered $\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots
\le\lambda_n$ and corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors $\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_n$. Then for
every $\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}$,
$$
\lambda_1\le R_A(\mathbf{x})\le\lambda_n,
$$ {#eq-rayleigh-bounds}
and
$$
\lambda_1=\min_{\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}}R_A(\mathbf{x})=R_A(\mathbf{q}_1),\qquad
\lambda_n=\max_{\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}}R_A(\mathbf{x})=R_A(\mathbf{q}_n).
$$
The minimum is attained exactly on the eigenspace $E_{\lambda_1}$, and the maximum exactly on
$E_{\lambda_n}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Expand $\mathbf{x}$ in the orthonormal eigenbasis, $\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\mathbf{q}_i$ with
$c_i=\mathbf{q}_i^\top\mathbf{x}$. Orthonormality gives $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}=\sum_i c_i^2$ and,
using $A\mathbf{q}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i$,
$$
\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i c_i^2 .
$$
Hence
$$
R_A(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_i c_i^2},
$$
a weighted average of the eigenvalues with weights $w_i=c_i^2/\sum_j c_j^2\ge 0$ summing to $1$. Any
weighted average lies between the smallest and largest values, giving @eq-rayleigh-bounds. Equality on
the right, $R_A(\mathbf{x})=\lambda_n$, forces all weight onto coordinates with $\lambda_i=\lambda_n$,
that is, $c_i=0$ whenever $\lambda_i<\lambda_n$, which says exactly $\mathbf{x}\in E_{\lambda_n}$;
taking $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{q}_n$ shows the value $\lambda_n$ is attained. The minimum statement is the
same argument with the inequality reversed. $\square$
:::

A one-line numeric check on the running matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$,
whose eigenvalues are $1$ and $3$: pointing along $\mathbf{e}_1=(1,0)^\top$ gives
$R_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}(\mathbf{e}_1)=\frac{2}{1}=2$, strictly inside $[1,3]$ as @eq-rayleigh-bounds
demands; pointing along the contrast $(1,-1)^\top$ gives $R_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\frac{2}{2}=1=\lambda_1$,
so the indirect-comparison direction is exactly the *minimum-variance* direction, and pointing along
$(1,1)^\top$ gives $\frac{6}{2}=3=\lambda_2$, the maximum.

::: {.remark}
**Rayleigh and principal component analysis.** Principal component analysis (PCA) looks for the direction
$\mathbf{x}$ with $\|\mathbf{x}\|=1$ that maximizes the variance $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{X})=
\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{x}$ of the projected data. By @thm-rayleigh that maximizer is the
top eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_n$ of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and the maximal variance is the top eigenvalue
$\lambda_n$. The first principal component is therefore an eigenvector, which is the link between this
theorem and the one eigenvalue idea most health researchers have already met. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Why this matters.** @eq-rayleigh-bounds says the variance of *any* contrast lies between the smallest
and largest eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, so the extreme eigenvalues bracket every possible
indirect-comparison variance at once. The top eigenvalue and eigenvector are exactly the first principal
component.

The extreme eigenvalues solve an unconstrained problem. The *interior* eigenvalues solve a min-max
problem over subspaces, the Courant-Fischer theorem, which we also prove in full. It needs no calculus,
only the spectral theorem and a dimension count. This is a supporting result; a first reader can take its
statement on faith and skip the proof.

In words, the first formula below says: among all $k$-dimensional subspaces $S$, look inside each one for
the *largest* Rayleigh value it contains, then pick the $S$ that makes that largest value as *small* as
possible; the answer is the $k$-th eigenvalue $\lambda_k$, achieved by the span of the bottom $k$
eigenvectors. The reason to care about these interior eigenvalues is that they control the middle
principal components and underlie the eigenvalue interlacing results used in dimension reduction and in
the stability analysis of estimated covariance matrices.

::: {#thm-courant-fischer}
## Courant-Fischer min-max theorem

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$. For
each $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$,
$$
\lambda_k=\min_{\substack{S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\\ \dim S=k}}\ \max_{\substack{\mathbf{x}\in S\\
\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}}}R_A(\mathbf{x})
=\max_{\substack{S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\\ \dim S=n-k+1}}\ \min_{\substack{\mathbf{x}\in S\\
\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}}}R_A(\mathbf{x}),
$$ {#eq-courant-fischer}
where $S$ ranges over subspaces of the stated dimension.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_n$ be orthonormal eigenvectors with $A\mathbf{q}_i=\lambda_i
\mathbf{q}_i$. We prove the first equality; the second follows by applying the first to $-A$, whose
eigenvalues are $-\lambda_n\le\cdots\le-\lambda_1$.

*Upper bound.* Take the particular subspace $S_0=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}$, of
dimension $k$. Every $\mathbf{x}\in S_0$ is $\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i\le k}c_i\mathbf{q}_i$, and as in
@thm-rayleigh,
$$
R_A(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_{i\le k}c_i^2}\le\lambda_k,
$$
because every $\lambda_i$ with $i\le k$ satisfies $\lambda_i\le\lambda_k$. Hence
$\max_{\mathbf{0}\ne\mathbf{x}\in S_0}R_A(\mathbf{x})\le\lambda_k$, so the minimum over all $k$-dimensional
$S$ is at most $\lambda_k$.

*Lower bound.* Let $S$ be any $k$-dimensional subspace and let $T=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{q}_k,
\mathbf{q}_{k+1},\dots,\mathbf{q}_n\}$, of dimension $n-k+1$. By the dimension formula
(@thm-rank-nullity),
$$
\dim(S\cap T)\ge\dim S+\dim T-n=k+(n-k+1)-n=1,
$$
so there is a nonzero $\mathbf{x}\in S\cap T$. Since $\mathbf{x}\in T$, $\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i\ge k}c_i
\mathbf{q}_i$ and
$$
R_A(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\sum_{i\ge k}\lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_{i\ge k}c_i^2}\ge\lambda_k,
$$
because every $\lambda_i$ with $i\ge k$ satisfies $\lambda_i\ge\lambda_k$. Therefore
$\max_{\mathbf{0}\ne\mathbf{x}\in S}R_A(\mathbf{x})\ge R_A(\mathbf{x})\ge\lambda_k$ for this particular
$\mathbf{x}$, and since $S$ was arbitrary, the minimum over all $k$-dimensional $S$ is at least
$\lambda_k$.

The two bounds coincide, giving the first equality in @eq-courant-fischer. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
The Rayleigh principle is the source of two facts used later; both can be deferred on a first reading.
The **operator $2$-norm** $\|A\|_2=\max_{\|\mathbf{x}\|=1}\|A\mathbf{x}\|$ is the largest factor by which
$A$ can stretch any unit vector. First, for symmetric $A$ this operator $2$-norm equals the largest
eigenvalue in magnitude, $\|A\|_2=\max_i|\lambda_i|$, while $\max_{\|\mathbf{x}\|=1}\mathbf{x}^\top
A\mathbf{x}=\lambda_n$; the two agree when $A\succeq 0$. Second, Courant-Fischer yields Weyl's monotonicity inequality, that
adding a positive semidefinite perturbation can only raise eigenvalues, which underlies the stability of
estimated covariance matrices. Both are pursued in the exercises. The bound @eq-rayleigh-bounds is also
a quantitative companion to the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-ip), specialized from
the standard inner product to the quadratic-form geometry of $A$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The singular value decomposition {#sec-la3-svd}

We now return to the situation that actually occurs in regression and evidence synthesis, where the data
matrix is not square and symmetric. A design matrix has one row per patient or per study-arm summary and
one column per covariate or model term, so it is rectangular, and the spectral theorem, which applies only
to symmetric and hence square matrices, does not reach it. We need a structure theorem for an arbitrary
$A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. The singular value decomposition supplies it, and it follows from the
spectral theorem applied to the symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $A^\top A$. Its singular values
will tell us, in plain terms, whether the available data actually support the directions in covariate
space that we are trying to estimate.

::: {#lem-ata-psd}
## $A^\top A$ is symmetric positive semidefinite

For any $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, the matrix $A^\top A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is symmetric and
positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative. Moreover $\mathcal{N}(A^\top A)=
\mathcal{N}(A)$, hence $\mathrm{rank}(A^\top A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Symmetry is $(A^\top A)^\top=A^\top A$. For any $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}^\top(A^\top A)\mathbf{x}=
(A\mathbf{x})^\top(A\mathbf{x})=\|A\mathbf{x}\|^2\ge 0$, so $A^\top A\succeq 0$, and
@thm-pd-characterization gives nonnegative eigenvalues. If $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ then $A^\top
A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$; conversely if $A^\top A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ then $0=\mathbf{x}^\top A^\top
A\mathbf{x}=\|A\mathbf{x}\|^2$ forces $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$. Thus the null spaces coincide, and by
the rank-nullity theorem (@thm-rank-nullity) the ranks agree. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-svd}
## Singular value decomposition

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ have rank $r$. Then there exist orthogonal matrices
$U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ and $V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and a matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times
n}$ that is zero off the main diagonal, with diagonal entries
$$
\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0=\sigma_{r+1}=\cdots=\sigma_{\min(m,n)},
$$
such that
$$
A=U\Sigma V^\top .
$$ {#eq-svd}
The numbers $\sigma_i$, the **singular values** of $A$, are uniquely determined by $A$ as
$\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i(A^\top A)}$ with the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ in decreasing order. The columns
of $V$ (the **right singular vectors**) are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A^\top A$, and the columns of
$U$ (the **left singular vectors**) are orthonormal eigenvectors of $AA^\top$.
:::

Before the proof, here is the story the three matrices tell. Read $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ right to left as a
pipeline acting on an input vector. The rotation $V^\top$ lines up the special *input* directions, the
right singular vectors $\mathbf{v}_j$, with the coordinate axes; $\Sigma$ stretches the $j$-th axis by
the factor $\sigma_j$, or annihilates it when $\sigma_j=0$; and the rotation $U$ places the stretched
axes along the *output* directions, the left singular vectors $\mathbf{u}_j$. The net effect is that $A$
sends each input direction $\mathbf{v}_j$ to $\sigma_j\mathbf{u}_j$: input axis in, stretched output axis
out. The singular values are the stretch factors, and a small $\sigma_j$ means $A$ barely moves that
input direction, the signature of a direction the data weakly support. The definition
$\mathbf{u}_j=\sigma_j^{-1}A\mathbf{v}_j$ in the proof is just this sentence written as an equation.

::: {.proof}
By @lem-ata-psd the matrix $A^\top A$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, so by @thm-spectral-theorem
there is an orthogonal $V=[\mathbf{v}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{v}_n]$ with
$$
A^\top A=V\Lambda V^\top,\qquad \Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n),\quad
\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge 0 .
$$
By @lem-ata-psd, $\mathrm{rank}(A^\top A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)=r$, and the rank of a diagonalized symmetric
matrix is the number of nonzero eigenvalues, so exactly $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r>0$ and
$\lambda_{r+1}=\cdots=\lambda_n=0$. Define $\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$, so $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r
>0$.

For $i=1,\dots,r$ define $\mathbf{u}_i=\sigma_i^{-1}A\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathbb{R}^m$. These are orthonormal:
$$
\mathbf{u}_i^\top\mathbf{u}_j=\frac{1}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}\mathbf{v}_i^\top A^\top A\mathbf{v}_j
=\frac{1}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}\mathbf{v}_i^\top(\lambda_j\mathbf{v}_j)
=\frac{\lambda_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}\,\delta_{ij}=\frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}\,\delta_{ij}
=\delta_{ij},
$$
using $A^\top A\mathbf{v}_j=\lambda_j\mathbf{v}_j$ and $\mathbf{v}_i^\top\mathbf{v}_j=\delta_{ij}$.
Extend $\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_r$ to an orthonormal basis $\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_m$ of
$\mathbb{R}^m$ by Gram-Schmidt (@thm-gram-schmidt), and set $U=[\mathbf{u}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{u}_m]$,
which is orthogonal. Let $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ have $\Sigma_{ii}=\sigma_i$ for $i\le r$ and
all other entries zero.

We verify $AV=U\Sigma$, which is equivalent to @eq-svd after multiplying on the right by $V^\top$. The
$j$-th column of $AV$ is $A\mathbf{v}_j$. For $j\le r$, $A\mathbf{v}_j=\sigma_j\mathbf{u}_j$ by the
definition of $\mathbf{u}_j$. For $j>r$, $\lambda_j=0$, so $\|A\mathbf{v}_j\|^2=\mathbf{v}_j^\top A^\top
A\mathbf{v}_j=\lambda_j=0$, giving $A\mathbf{v}_j=\mathbf{0}$. The $j$-th column of $U\Sigma$ is
$\sigma_j\mathbf{u}_j$ for $j\le r$ and $\mathbf{0}$ for $j>r$. The columns match, so $AV=U\Sigma$ and
$A=U\Sigma V^\top$.

*Uniqueness of the singular values.* From @eq-svd, $A^\top A=V\Sigma^\top U^\top U\Sigma V^\top=
V(\Sigma^\top\Sigma)V^\top$, and $\Sigma^\top\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\dots,\sigma_r^2,0,\dots,0)$.
This exhibits the $\sigma_i^2$ as the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$, which depend only on $A$; hence the
$\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i(A^\top A)}$ are determined by $A$. Finally $AA^\top=U\Sigma V^\top V\Sigma^\top
U^\top=U(\Sigma\Sigma^\top)U^\top$ shows the columns of $U$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $AA^\top$,
with the same nonzero eigenvalues $\sigma_i^2$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Geometry and the four subspaces.** The decomposition @eq-svd says that, in the right orthonormal
input basis $\{\mathbf{v}_j\}$ and output basis $\{\mathbf{u}_i\}$, $A$ acts diagonally: it stretches by
$\sigma_i$ along paired axes and annihilates the rest. The image of the unit sphere under $A$ is an
ellipsoid with semi-axes $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$ along $\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_r$, so
$\sigma_1=\|A\|_2$ is the operator norm and $\sigma_r$ measures how close $A$ is to dropping rank. The
singular vectors lay bare the four fundamental subspaces of @thm-four-subspaces:
$\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_r\}$ is an orthonormal basis of the column space $\mathcal{C}(A)$,
$\{\mathbf{u}_{r+1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_m\}$ of the left null space $\mathcal{N}(A^\top)$,
$\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_r\}$ of the row space $\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$, and
$\{\mathbf{v}_{r+1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_n\}$ of the null space $\mathcal{N}(A)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The same four-subspaces correspondence is easier to hold in a table.

| Fundamental subspace | Lives in | Spanned by | Dimension | Plain meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| column space $\mathcal{C}(A)$ | $\mathbb{R}^m$ | $\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_r$ | $r$ | output directions $A$ can reach |
| left null space $\mathcal{N}(A^\top)$ | $\mathbb{R}^m$ | $\mathbf{u}_{r+1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_m$ | $m-r$ | output directions never reached |
| row space $\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$ | $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_r$ | $r$ | input directions that matter |
| null space $\mathcal{N}(A)$ | $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $\mathbf{v}_{r+1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_n$ | $n-r$ | input directions $A$ ignores |

To picture the "unit sphere maps to an ellipsoid" claim without a figure, track a few unit inputs through
the symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose singular values equal its eigenvalues
$3$ and $1$. The output lengths trace out an ellipse with semi-axes $3$ and $1$.

| Unit input direction | Output | Output length |
|---|---|---|
| $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ | $(3,3)/\sqrt2$ | $3$ (long axis) |
| $(1,0)$ | $(2,1)$ | $\sqrt5\approx 2.24$ |
| $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ | $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ | $1$ (short axis) |

The longest stretch is $\sigma_1=3$ and the shortest is $\sigma_r=1$; their ratio is the single most
useful diagnostic in applied regression, so we name it.

::: {#def-condition-number}
## Condition number

For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ of rank $r$ with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, the
**condition number** (in the $2$-norm) is
$$
\kappa(A)=\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_r}.
$$
For a full-rank square $A$ this equals $\|A\|_2\,\|A^{-1}\|_2$.
:::

**Reader translation.** The condition number compares the largest stretch to the smallest. When it is
close to $1$, $A$ treats all directions evenly and is easy to invert; when it is large, some input
direction is barely stretched, so undoing $A$ blows up tiny errors in that direction.

**Why this matters.** This is the fact a health researcher fitting a regression most needs. A design
matrix $\mathbf{X}$ with two nearly collinear covariates has a tiny smallest singular value, hence a huge
$\kappa(\mathbf{X})$. Because $\kappa(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\kappa(\mathbf{X})^2$, the Gram matrix is
then nearly singular, and the variance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$, which scales with
$(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, is inflated along the ill-supported direction. Large condition number
is the linear-algebra name for collinearity and variance inflation.

One more size measure, used in the exercises, fits naturally here. The **Frobenius norm** of
$A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ is $\|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2}=\sqrt{\sum_i\sigma_i^2}$, the Euclidean
length of $A$ when its entries are read as one long vector; the second equality, which expresses it
through the singular values, is proved in @exr-frobenius-singular.

## The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse {#sec-la3-pseudoinverse}

When $A$ is square and invertible, $A^{-1}$ solves $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ uniquely. When $A$ is
rectangular or rank-deficient, no inverse exists, yet we still want a canonical operator that "best
undoes" $A$. This is the everyday situation in evidence synthesis: the design has too few independent
data directions to pin down every coefficient, the covariates are collinear, or several coefficient
vectors fit the data equally well. The pseudoinverse is the principled replacement for the missing
inverse in all three cases. The singular value decomposition delivers it by inverting only the nonzero
stretching factors and leaving the unsupported directions alone. The formal four-equation
characterization comes after the definition, but the practical message is exactly this paragraph.

::: {#def-pseudoinverse}
## Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ have singular value decomposition $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ as in @thm-svd.
The **Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ is
$$
A^{+}=V\Sigma^{+}U^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m},
$$ {#eq-pseudoinverse}
where $\Sigma^{+}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ is the matrix with $(\Sigma^{+})_{ii}=\sigma_i^{-1}$ for
$i=1,\dots,r$ and all other entries zero. Equivalently $A^{+}=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i^{-1}\mathbf{v}_i
\mathbf{u}_i^\top$.
:::

**Reader translation.** The pseudoinverse runs the SVD pipeline backwards, but only on the directions
that were genuinely stretched. It un-rotates with $U^\top$, divides by $\sigma_i$ on the $r$ supported
axes and does nothing on the rest (you cannot divide by the zero stretch of an unsupported direction),
then un-rotates with $V$. It inverts what can be inverted and quietly leaves the null directions alone.

The formula uses a particular singular value decomposition, of which there may be many. The next
proposition shows the result does not depend on that choice, by characterizing $A^{+}$ intrinsically
through four equations.

::: {#prp-pseudoinverse-penrose}
## The Penrose equations characterize $A^{+}$

The matrix $X=A^{+}$ of @def-pseudoinverse satisfies the four **Penrose equations**
$$
\text{(P1) } AXA=A,\quad \text{(P2) } XAX=X,\quad \text{(P3) } (AX)^\top=AX,\quad \text{(P4) }
(XA)^\top=XA,
$$
and it is the only matrix that does so. In particular $A^{+}$ is independent of the chosen singular
value decomposition. If $A$ is invertible then $A^{+}=A^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Existence.* With $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ and $X=V\Sigma^{+}U^\top$, orthogonality of $U,V$ gives
$$
AX=U\Sigma\Sigma^{+}U^\top,\qquad XA=V\Sigma^{+}\Sigma V^\top .
$$
Now $\Sigma\Sigma^{+}=\mathrm{diag}(I_r,\mathbf{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ and $\Sigma^{+}\Sigma=
\mathrm{diag}(I_r,\mathbf{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ are diagonal with $0/1$ entries, hence
