symmetric, so $AX$ and $XA$ are symmetric, giving (P3) and (P4). Because
$\Sigma\Sigma^{+}\Sigma=\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^{+}\Sigma\Sigma^{+}=\Sigma^{+}$ (a $0/1$ diagonal scaling
fixes the matched diagonal entries), we get $AXA=U\Sigma\Sigma^{+}\Sigma V^\top=U\Sigma V^\top=A$, which
is (P1), and $XAX=V\Sigma^{+}\Sigma\Sigma^{+}U^\top=V\Sigma^{+}U^\top=X$, which is (P2).

*Uniqueness.* Suppose $G$ and $H$ each satisfy (P1) to (P4) for $A$. We take the chains one short step at
a time, writing the rule used on the right. First we show $AG=AH$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
AG &= (AG)^\top && \text{(P3 for }G\text{)}\\
   &= G^\top A^\top && \text{(transpose of a product)}\\
   &= G^\top (AHA)^\top && \text{(P1 for }H\text{: }A=AHA)\\
   &= G^\top A^\top H^\top A^\top && \text{(transpose of a product)}\\
   &= (AG)^\top (AH)^\top && \text{(regroup }G^\top A^\top,\ H^\top A^\top)\\
   &= (AG)(AH) && \text{(P3 for }G\text{ and }H)\\
   &= (AGA)H = AH && \text{(P1 for }G).
\end{aligned}
$$
Symmetrically, using (P4) and (P1), we show $GA=HA$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
GA &= (GA)^\top && \text{(P4 for }G\text{)}\\
   &= A^\top G^\top && \text{(transpose of a product)}\\
   &= (AHA)^\top G^\top && \text{(P1 for }H\text{: }A=AHA)\\
   &= A^\top H^\top A^\top G^\top && \text{(transpose of a product)}\\
   &= (HA)^\top (GA)^\top && \text{(regroup }A^\top H^\top,\ A^\top G^\top)\\
   &= (HA)(GA) && \text{(P4 for }H\text{ and }G)\\
   &= H(AGA) = HA && \text{(P1 for }G).
\end{aligned}
$$
Now combine with (P2):
$$
\begin{aligned}
G &= GAG && \text{(P2 for }G\text{)}\\
  &= G(AG) = G(AH) && \text{(}AG=AH\text{ above)}\\
  &= (GA)H = (HA)H && \text{(}GA=HA\text{ above)}\\
  &= H(AH) = HAH = H && \text{(P2 for }H).
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence the matrix satisfying the four equations is unique; since $A^{+}$ satisfies them and they do not
mention the decomposition, $A^{+}$ is well defined. If $A$ is invertible, $X=A^{-1}$ satisfies all four
equations (each reduces to a trivial identity), so by uniqueness $A^{+}=A^{-1}$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** The four equations pin down $A^{+}$ with no reference to any particular singular
value decomposition, so "the pseudoinverse" is a single well-defined object rather than an artifact of a
choice. And because it collapses to $A^{-1}$ whenever the ordinary inverse exists, it is a genuine
extension of the inverse, safe to use as a drop-in replacement throughout regression.

The pseudoinverse is intimately tied to orthogonal projection, which is where Chapter 2 re-enters.

::: {#prp-pseudoinverse-projection}
## Pseudoinverse and orthogonal projection

For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, the matrix $AA^{+}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb{R}^m$
onto the column space $\mathcal{C}(A)$, and $A^{+}A$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb{R}^n$
onto the row space $\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$. When $A$ has full column rank $r=n$, the Gram matrix
$A^\top A$ is invertible and
$$
A^{+}=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top,\qquad AA^{+}=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
With $A=U\Sigma V^\top$, write $U_r=[\mathbf{u}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{u}_r]$ for the first $r$ left singular
vectors. From the proof of @prp-pseudoinverse-penrose, $AA^{+}=U\,\mathrm{diag}(I_r,\mathbf{0})\,U^\top=
U_rU_r^\top$. The columns of $U_r$ are orthonormal and, by the remark after @thm-svd, form a basis of
$\mathcal{C}(A)$. By the projection theorem (@thm-projection-theorem) and the orthonormal-basis formula
for a projection matrix (@def-projection-matrix), $U_rU_r^\top$ is exactly the orthogonal projection
onto $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_r\}=\mathcal{C}(A)$. The same argument applied to
$A^{+}A=V_rV_r^\top$ identifies it with the orthogonal projection onto
$\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_r\}=\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$.

If $r=n$, then $A^\top A\succ 0$ by @lem-ata-psd and the remark after @thm-pd-characterization, hence
invertible. The matrix $M=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$ satisfies the four Penrose equations: $AM=A(A^\top
A)^{-1}A^\top$ is symmetric and $MA=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top A=I_n$ is symmetric, giving (P3), (P4);
$AMA=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top A=A$ gives (P1); and $MAM=I_n M=M$ gives (P2). By the uniqueness in
@prp-pseudoinverse-penrose, $A^{+}=M=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$, and $AA^{+}=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** Multiplying by $A^{+}$ and then by $A$ is geometry: $AA^{+}$ projects onto the
column space (the fitted values a model can produce), and $A^{+}A$ projects onto the row space (the part
of the coefficients the data can identify). This is the bridge from the abstract pseudoinverse to the
familiar machinery of least squares.

The formula $A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$ is precisely the hat matrix of least squares, which Chapter 6
studies in depth; here it appears as a special case of the pseudoinverse. The pseudoinverse also solves
the general least-squares problem, even when the solution is not unique, by selecting the solution of
minimum norm.

::: {#prp-pseudoinverse-lstsq}
## Minimum-norm least-squares solution

For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^m$, the vector $\mathbf{x}^\star=A^{+}
\mathbf{b}$ minimizes $\|A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}\|$ over all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and among all
minimizers it is the unique one of smallest Euclidean norm.
:::

::: {.proof}
Using the orthogonal $U$, $\|A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}\|=\|U^\top(A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b})\|=\|\Sigma
V^\top\mathbf{x}-U^\top\mathbf{b}\|$. Put $\mathbf{z}=V^\top\mathbf{x}$ (a bijective change of variable
preserving norm, since $\|\mathbf{x}\|=\|\mathbf{z}\|$) and $\mathbf{c}=U^\top\mathbf{b}$. Then
$$
\|A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^r(\sigma_i z_i-c_i)^2+\sum_{i=r+1}^m c_i^2 .
$$
The second sum is fixed. The first is minimized, to zero, exactly by $z_i=c_i/\sigma_i$ for $i\le r$;
the coordinates $z_{r+1},\dots,z_n$ are free and do not affect the residual. Among these minimizers,
$\|\mathbf{x}\|^2=\|\mathbf{z}\|^2=\sum_{i\le r}(c_i/\sigma_i)^2+\sum_{i>r}z_i^2$ is smallest exactly
when the free coordinates are zero. That choice gives $\mathbf{z}=\Sigma^{+}\mathbf{c}$, hence
$\mathbf{x}^\star=V\mathbf{z}=V\Sigma^{+}U^\top\mathbf{b}=A^{+}\mathbf{b}$, and it is unique. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation.** "Minimum norm" is not arbitrary. When several coefficient vectors fit the data
equally well, they differ only by directions the data cannot see (the null space of $A$). Among all those
equally good fits, the pseudoinverse returns the one of smallest Euclidean length, which is the one that
adds nothing in the unsupported directions. It is the honest answer: it refuses to invent coefficient
values that the data do not constrain.

## Covariance matrices are symmetric and positive semidefinite {#sec-la3-covariance}

The objects of this chapter are not abstract: the covariance matrix of any random vector is symmetric
positive semidefinite, which is why the entire spectral machinery transfers directly to statistics.

::: {.remark}
**Bridge to Chapter 4.** Let $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ be a random vector with finite second moments
and mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}]$. Its covariance matrix
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X})=\mathbb{E}\!\big[(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})
(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\big]
$$
is symmetric, because $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^\top=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ entrywise, and positive
semidefinite, because for any fixed $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{a}
=\mathbb{E}\!\big[\big(\mathbf{a}^\top(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\big)^2\big]
=\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{X})\ge 0 .
$$
This is proved as @thm-cov-psd in Chapter 4. Three consequences of the present chapter then apply
verbatim. By @thm-spectral-theorem, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis;
the eigenvectors are the principal axes of variation and the eigenvalues the variances along them, which
is principal component analysis. By @prp-matrix-square-root, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ has a symmetric
positive semidefinite square root, and when $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$ the whitening transform
$\mathbf{Z}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ has covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}=I_n$. The induced norm
$\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}=\sqrt{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}$ is
the Mahalanobis distance that the matching methods of Part V use to compare covariate profiles across
studies. In words, it is the standardized distance that accounts for correlation and unequal variances:
two covariate profiles that differ by one raw unit count as far apart along directions in which the study
has little variation, and close along directions in which it has a lot. Whitening makes this precise,
since $\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}=\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\mathbf{x}\|_2$ is ordinary
Euclidean distance after the data have been whitened. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A fully worked example {#sec-la3-example}

We carry one small symmetric matrix through the whole theory, then treat a rank-deficient rectangular
matrix to see the singular value decomposition and pseudoinverse in action. Every number below is
checkable by hand.

**A symmetric $2\times 2$ matrix.** Let
$$
A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.
$$
This is exactly the running covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ of @exm-la3-contrast-covariance for the two
correlated log-odds-ratio estimates $(\hat y_{AB},\hat y_{AC})$; we call it $A$ here to match the
eigen-computation notation and read each result back as a statement about the indirect comparison.

*Eigenvalues.* The characteristic polynomial is
$$
\chi_A(t)=\det\!\begin{pmatrix} t-2 & -1\\ -1 & t-2\end{pmatrix}=(t-2)^2-1=t^2-4t+3=(t-1)(t-3),
$$
so $\lambda_1=1$ and $\lambda_2=3$. As a check, $\mathrm{tr}(A)=2+2=4=1+3$ and
$\det(A)=4-1=3=1\cdot 3$, matching @lem-trace-det-eigenvalues.

*Eigenvectors and the spectral decomposition.* For $\lambda=3$, $(A-3I)\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\
1&-1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives $\mathbf{v}\propto(1,1)$; for $\lambda=1$, $(A-I)\mathbf{v}=
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives $\mathbf{v}\propto(1,-1)$. The two are
orthogonal, as @lem-sym-orthogonal-eigenvectors promises. Normalizing,
$$
\mathbf{q}_{3}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{q}_{1}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
Q=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\Lambda=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
$$
and one verifies $Q\Lambda Q^\top=A$ directly: $Q\Lambda=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\3&-1
\end{pmatrix}$, and $(Q\Lambda)Q^\top=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\
1&-1\end{pmatrix}=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}=A$.

*Definiteness.* Both eigenvalues are positive, so $A\succ 0$ by @thm-pd-characterization. The leading
principal minors are $\Delta_1=2>0$ and $\Delta_2=\det A=3>0$, confirming positive definiteness through
@thm-sylvester-criterion as well.

*Rayleigh quotient.* By @thm-rayleigh, $R_A$ ranges over $[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]=[1,3]$. The maximum is
attained at $\mathbf{q}_3$: with $\mathbf{x}=(1,1)$, $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=(1,1)\binom{3}{3}=6$
and $\|\mathbf{x}\|^2=2$, so $R_A=3$. The minimum is attained at $\mathbf{q}_1$: with $\mathbf{x}=
(1,-1)$, $\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=(1,-1)\binom{1}{-1}=2$ and $\|\mathbf{x}\|^2=2$, so $R_A=1$. A
generic direction sits strictly inside: $\mathbf{x}=(1,0)$ gives $R_A=2/1=2\in(1,3)$.

*Square root.* By @prp-matrix-square-root, $A^{1/2}=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt3,1)\,Q^\top$. Writing
$a=\tfrac{\sqrt3+1}{2}$ and $b=\tfrac{\sqrt3-1}{2}$,
$$
A^{1/2}=\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ b & a\end{pmatrix}.
$$
We confirm $(A^{1/2})^2=A$ by hand: $a^2+b^2=\tfrac{(\sqrt3+1)^2+(\sqrt3-1)^2}{4}=\tfrac{8}{4}=2$ and
$2ab=2\cdot\tfrac{(\sqrt3+1)(\sqrt3-1)}{4}=2\cdot\tfrac{2}{4}=1$, so
$(A^{1/2})^2=\begin{pmatrix}a^2+b^2 & 2ab\\ 2ab & a^2+b^2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2
\end{pmatrix}=A$.

*Indirect-comparison reading.* Now read these numbers as facts about the two correlated estimates
$(\hat y_{AB},\hat y_{AC})$ with covariance $A=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. The two estimates have correlation
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}}=1/2$. The variance of
the Bucher indirect comparison $\hat d_{BC}=\hat y_{AB}-\hat y_{AC}$ is the quadratic form along the
contrast $\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^\top$,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat d_{BC})=\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=2 .
$$
The two eigenpairs are the principal axes of uncertainty: the high-variance axis $\mathbf{q}_3=(1,1)/
\sqrt2$ with variance $\lambda=3$ is the direction in which both estimates move together, and the
low-variance axis $\mathbf{q}_1=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ with variance $\lambda=1$ is the contrast direction. The
indirect comparison therefore lies on the *better-determined* axis of the pair. The condition number is
$\kappa(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\sigma_1/\sigma_2=3/1=3$, comfortably small, so this two-estimate problem is
well conditioned. For the Mahalanobis distance and whitening, invert and take the square root through the
spectrum:
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}
=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}=Q\,\mathrm{diag}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},1\big)\,Q^\top ,
$$
so the whitened vector $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\hat{\mathbf y}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ has covariance
$I_2$: whitening rescales the variance-$3$ axis and the variance-$1$ axis to equal variance $1$, removing
the correlation. This single matrix has now illustrated eigenvalues, the spectral decomposition,
definiteness, the Rayleigh bounds, the square root, contrast variance, conditioning, and the Mahalanobis
metric, each as a concrete statement about an indirect comparison.

**A rank-deficient matrix.** Let
$$
C=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix},
$$
whose rows are proportional, so $\mathrm{rank}(C)=1$.

*Singular values and vectors.* Compute $C^\top C=\begin{pmatrix}5&10\\10&20\end{pmatrix}$, with
$\mathrm{tr}=25$ and $\det=100-100=0$, hence eigenvalues $\lambda=25$ and $\lambda=0$. The single
nonzero singular value is $\sigma_1=\sqrt{25}=5$. The right singular vector solves
$(C^\top C-25I)\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}-20&10\\10&-5\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$, giving
$\mathbf{v}_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(1,2)$. The left singular vector is $\mathbf{u}_1=\sigma_1^{-1}C
\mathbf{v}_1=\tfrac{1}{5}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\binom{1+4}{2+8}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\binom{1}{2}$.

*Pseudoinverse.* By @def-pseudoinverse, $C^{+}=\sigma_1^{-1}\mathbf{v}_1\mathbf{u}_1^\top=
\tfrac{1}{5}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\binom{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(1\ \ 2)=\tfrac{1}{25}
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}=\tfrac{1}{25}C$. We verify the Penrose identity (P1) of
@prp-pseudoinverse-penrose. Since $C^2=\begin{pmatrix}5&10\\10&20\end{pmatrix}=5C$, we have $C^3=5C^2=
25C$, so
$$
CC^{+}C=C\cdot\tfrac{1}{25}C\cdot C=\tfrac{1}{25}C^3=\tfrac{1}{25}(25C)=C,
$$
as required. The projection $CC^{+}=\tfrac{1}{25}C^2=\tfrac{1}{25}(5C)=\tfrac15 C=\tfrac15
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric and idempotent, and it is the orthogonal projection
onto $\mathcal{C}(C)=\mathrm{span}\{(1,2)\}$, in agreement with @prp-pseudoinverse-projection.

*Conditioning reading.* The matrix $C$ has singular values $\sigma_1=5$ and $\sigma_2=0$, so its
condition number is infinite: the two rows are exactly proportional, and the data carry no information at
all along the second input direction $\mathbf{v}_2=(2,-1)/\sqrt5$. This is perfect collinearity, the
extreme case of @def-condition-number. A real design matrix with two *nearly* collinear covariates would
have a small but nonzero $\sigma_2$, hence a large finite condition number, and the variance of the
corresponding coefficient would be inflated by roughly $1/\sigma_2^2$. The pseudoinverse keeps the
problem well posed by simply declining to invert the zero (or near-zero) direction.

## Notes and references {#sec-la3-notes}

The material of this chapter is classical linear algebra. The eigenvalue and diagonalization theory,
the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, positive definite matrices and Sylvester's criterion, the
singular value decomposition, and the pseudoinverse are all developed in @strang2016, which is our
standing reference for the field; the determinant facts and the existence and extension of bases that we
cite without proof are established there. The fundamental theorem of algebra, used once to guarantee
that the characteristic polynomial has a complex root, is the only genuinely analytic prerequisite and
is standard.

The inductive proof of the spectral theorem given here, peeling off one real eigenvector and restricting
to its $A$-invariant orthogonal complement, is the most self-contained route and avoids the machinery of
Schur factorization. The variational results, @thm-rayleigh and the Courant-Fischer theorem
@thm-courant-fischer, are proved by elementary weighted-average and dimension-count arguments rather
than by Lagrange multipliers, keeping the chapter free of calculus. Sylvester's criterion is proved by
an eigenvalue and dimension-count argument; an alternative proof through the $LDL^\top$ factorization,
in which the pivots equal the ratios of successive leading minors, is outlined in @strang2016.

These linear-algebra primitives have no separate counterpart in the companion `ITC_Coq` development,
whose formalized theorems live at the causal and statistical layer rather than at the level of matrix
factorizations; accordingly, none of the results here carries a machine-checked tag. The downstream uses
foreshadowed in @sec-la3-covariance, namely the positive semidefiniteness of covariance matrices and the
Mahalanobis distance, reappear in the probability chapter and in the distance-matching methods of
Part V.

## Exercises {#sec-la3-exercises}

An exercise marked with a star $\star$ has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The set is ordered
roughly from warm-up and interpretation through computation to proof, so start at the top and stop where
the difficulty outruns your current need.

::: {#exr-la3-eigen-warmup}
## Warm-up: check an eigenpair without the characteristic polynomial

(Warm-up.) Let $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. By direct multiplication only,
verify that $(1,1)^\top$ and $(1,-1)^\top$ are eigenvectors and read off their eigenvalues. Which of the
two directions carries the larger variance, and which one is the indirect-contrast direction
$\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^\top$? You should not need to compute a determinant.
:::

::: {#exr-la3-contrast-variance}
## Interpretation: covariance of two log-odds-ratio estimates

(Interpretation and computation.) Two trials sharing comparator $A$ give log-odds-ratio estimates with
covariance matrix
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}0.05 & 0.02\\ 0.02 & 0.05\end{pmatrix}
$$
(in convenient units). (a) Compute the correlation between the two estimates. (b) Using the quadratic
form $\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}$ with $\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^\top$, find the variance and
the standard error of the indirect comparison $\hat d_{BC}=\hat y_{AB}-\hat y_{AC}$. (c) Confirm
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$ with Sylvester's criterion (@thm-sylvester-criterion). (d) Find the
eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and state in one sentence which direction in the
$(\hat y_{AB},\hat y_{AC})$ plane is the most uncertain and which is the least.
:::

::: {#exr-la3-collinear-design}
## Interpretation: collinearity and the condition number

(Interpretation and computation.) Two covariates are standardized and have sample correlation $r=0.99$,
so their (scaled) Gram matrix is $G=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.99\\ 0.99 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the
eigenvalues of $G$ (recall that $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $a\pm b$). (b)
Compute the condition number $\kappa(G)=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$ of @def-condition-number. (c)
Explain in one or two sentences what the small eigenvalue says about how precisely the coefficient of the
$(1,-1)^\top$ direction can be estimated, and connect this to variance inflation under collinearity.
:::

::: {#exr-diagonalize-symmetric}
## Spectral decomposition by hand

Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. Find the eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, write
the spectral decomposition $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$, and verify $\mathrm{tr}(A)=\sum_i\lambda_i$ and
$\det(A)=\prod_i\lambda_i$. Compute $A^{1/2}$ and check that its square is $A$.
:::

::: {#exr-definiteness-test}
## Two definiteness tests

For each matrix decide whether it is positive definite, positive semidefinite but not definite, or
indefinite, using both the eigenvalue characterization (@thm-pd-characterization) and, where it
applies, Sylvester's criterion (@thm-sylvester-criterion):
$$
B_1=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Explain why Sylvester's criterion alone cannot certify the semidefinite case $B_2$.
:::

::: {#exr-svd-pseudoinverse}
## Singular value decomposition and pseudoinverse

Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2}$. Compute $A^\top A$, its
eigenvalues and eigenvectors, the singular values, a full singular value decomposition $A=U\Sigma
V^\top$, and the pseudoinverse $A^{+}$. Verify all four Penrose equations and confirm that $AA^{+}$ is
the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal{C}(A)$.
:::

::: {#exr-matrix-power-eigenvalues}
## Eigenvalues of powers and inverses

Let $A$ be symmetric with eigenpairs $(\lambda_i,\mathbf{q}_i)$. Prove that for every integer $k\ge 1$
the matrix $A^k$ is symmetric with eigenpairs $(\lambda_i^k,\mathbf{q}_i)$, and that if $A$ is invertible
then $A^{-1}$ has eigenpairs $(\lambda_i^{-1},\mathbf{q}_i)$. Deduce that $\mathrm{tr}(A^k)=\sum_i
\lambda_i^k$.
:::

::: {#exr-inverse-pd}
## Positive definiteness is inherited by the inverse and the root

Let $A\succ 0$ be symmetric. Prove that $A$ is invertible, that $A^{-1}\succ 0$, and that
$A^{1/2}\succ 0$. Prove moreover that if $A\succeq B\succeq 0$ with $A$ invertible then
$B^{1/2}A^{-1}B^{1/2}\preceq I$, and conclude $\det(B)\le\det(A)$.
:::

::: {#exr-rayleigh-max}
## Rayleigh maximization and uniqueness of the maximizer

Let $A$ be symmetric with largest eigenvalue $\lambda_n$. Prove that $\lambda_n=\max_{\|\mathbf{x}\|=1}
\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}$ and that the maximizer is unique up to sign if and only if $\lambda_n$ has
algebraic multiplicity one. Give an explicit symmetric $2\times 2$ matrix for which the maximizer is not
unique.
:::

::: {#exr-la3-penrose-rank-one}
## Computation: the Penrose equations for a rank-one matrix

(Computation.) Let $C=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, the rank-one matrix of the worked example,
whose pseudoinverse is $C^{+}=\tfrac{1}{25}C$. Verify all four Penrose equations (P1) to (P4) of
@prp-pseudoinverse-penrose directly, using $C^2=5C$. Then confirm that $CC^{+}$ is symmetric and
idempotent, so it is an orthogonal projection, and identify the subspace it projects onto. This is the
concrete warm-up for the abstract uniqueness argument and the starred exercises that follow.
:::

::: {#exr-ata-aat-spectrum}
## Shared spectrum of $A^\top A$ and $AA^\top$ (starred)

$\star$ (Proof.) Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. Prove that $A^\top A$ and $AA^\top$ have exactly
the same nonzero eigenvalues, with the same multiplicities, and that $\mathbf{v}\mapsto A\mathbf{v}$ maps
the eigenspace of $A^\top A$ for a nonzero $\lambda$ isomorphically onto the eigenspace of $AA^\top$ for
$\lambda$. Conclude that the nonzero singular values of $A$ and of $A^\top$ coincide, and that
$\|A\|_F^2:=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=\sum_i\sigma_i^2=\mathrm{tr}(A^\top A)$.
:::

::: {#exr-weyl-inequality}
## Weyl's inequality from the Rayleigh principle (starred)

$\star$ (Proof.) Let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues written in
increasing order, $\lambda_1(\cdot)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(\cdot)$. Using the Courant-Fischer theorem
(@thm-courant-fischer), prove Weyl's inequality
$$
\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_1(B)\le\lambda_k(A+B)\le\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_n(B),\qquad k=1,\dots,n.
$$
Deduce that if $B\succeq 0$ then $\lambda_k(A+B)\ge\lambda_k(A)$ for every $k$ (adding a positive
semidefinite matrix cannot decrease any eigenvalue), and that
$|\lambda_k(A+B)-\lambda_k(A)|\le\|B\|_2$ for every $k$.
:::

::: {#exr-frobenius-singular}
## Rank, Frobenius norm, and the best low-rank approximation

Let $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ have singular values $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$. Prove that
$\mathrm{rank}(A)$ equals the number of nonzero singular values and that $\|A\|_F^2=\sum_i\sigma_i^2$.
Define $A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{v}_i^\top$ for $k<r$. Prove directly that
$\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2$, and explain in one sentence why $A_k$ is a natural rank-$k$
approximation of $A$.
:::

::: {#exr-correlation-psd}
## Covariance and correlation matrices

Let $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ have covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. Prove from the definition
that $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and that $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$
unless some nontrivial linear combination $\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is almost surely constant. Show
that the correlation matrix $R$ with $R_{ij}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ii}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{jj}}$ is also positive semidefinite, and conclude that every correlation satisfies
$|R_{ij}|\le 1$.
:::
